name: english_set5_p1
label: English Language: set 5 (oral English: vowels, consonants, stress, intonation and listening)

papers.title: Vowels and Diphthongs: practice set 1
papers.description: 8 original WASSCE-style objective questions on vowels and diphthongs, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem:
Choose the word that has the same vowel sound as the one represented by the letters in bold.

f**oo**d
questions.explanation:
*Food* has the long vowel /uː/, the same sound as in *shoe*, *blue* and *true*. The spelling *oo* can stand for /uː/, /ʊ/ or /ʌ/, so listen to the sound, not the letters.

**Listen** (standard British English)

[food /fuːd/](https://wasscetutor.com/audio/oral/food.mp3?v=e2b81eb32a) [shoe /ʃuː/](https://wasscetutor.com/audio/oral/shoe.mp3?v=5278cb5a8e) [good /ɡʊd/](https://wasscetutor.com/audio/oral/good.mp3?v=b7a3537164) [blood /blʌd/](https://wasscetutor.com/audio/oral/blood.mp3?v=e1f6cc3451) [boat /bəʊt/](https://wasscetutor.com/audio/oral/boat.mp3?v=996143f877)

**Why the other options are wrong**

- good: *Good* has the short vowel /ʊ/, as in *put*, although it is spelt with *oo* like *food*.
- blood: *Blood* has /ʌ/, as in *cut*: another *oo* word that does not sound like *food*.
- boat: *Boat* has the diphthong /əʊ/, as in *go*.

questions.stem: Which of the following words has a different vowel sound from the others?
questions.explanation:
*Seize*, *field* and *key* all have the long vowel /iː/ of *see*. *Busy* is pronounced /ˈbɪzi/: its first vowel is the short /ɪ/ of *sit*, although it is spelt with *u*.

**Listen** (standard British English)

[busy /ˈbɪzi/](https://wasscetutor.com/audio/oral/busy.mp3?v=3ea3c98d5b) [seize /siːz/](https://wasscetutor.com/audio/oral/seize.mp3?v=001621b0ae) [field /fiːld/](https://wasscetutor.com/audio/oral/field.mp3?v=c7af2e5ee5) [key /kiː/](https://wasscetutor.com/audio/oral/key.mp3?v=83f54f5ecb)

**Why the other options are wrong**

- seize: *Seize* has /iː/, like the others.
- field: *Field* has /iː/, like the others.
- key: *Key* has /iː/, like the others.

questions.stem: Choose the word that rhymes with *blood*.
questions.explanation:
*Blood* is pronounced /blʌd/, with the vowel of *cut*, so it rhymes with *mud*, *flood* and *bud*. Rhyme depends on sound: *food* and *good* look like *blood* but do not rhyme with it.

**Listen** (standard British English)

[blood /blʌd/](https://wasscetutor.com/audio/oral/blood.mp3?v=e1f6cc3451) [mud /mʌd/](https://wasscetutor.com/audio/oral/mud.mp3?v=6b53f15e03) [food /fuːd/](https://wasscetutor.com/audio/oral/food.mp3?v=e2b81eb32a) [good /ɡʊd/](https://wasscetutor.com/audio/oral/good.mp3?v=b7a3537164) [road /rəʊd/](https://wasscetutor.com/audio/oral/road.mp3?v=7d8802edf8)

**Why the other options are wrong**

- food: *Food* ends in /uːd/, not /ʌd/.
- good: *Good* ends in /ʊd/, not /ʌd/.
- road: *Road* ends in /əʊd/, not /ʌd/.

questions.stem: Which of the following words contains a diphthong?
questions.explanation:
*Hair* has the diphthong /eə/: the tongue glides from /e/ towards /ə/. In a pure vowel the tongue stays in one position, as in *her*, *hat* and *heart*.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- her: *Her* has the pure long vowel /ɜː/.
- hat: *Hat* has the pure short vowel /æ/.
- heart: *Heart* has the pure long vowel /ɑː/.

questions.stem: In which of the following words is the letter in bold pronounced as the weak vowel /ə/ (schwa)?
questions.explanation:
The schwa /ə/ appears only in unstressed syllables. In *about* (/əˈbaʊt/) the stress falls on the second syllable, so the first *a* weakens to /ə/.

**Listen** (standard British English)

[about /əˈbaʊt/](https://wasscetutor.com/audio/oral/about.mp3?v=a5dce7a38a) [cat /kæt/](https://wasscetutor.com/audio/oral/cat.mp3?v=324bad803b) [father /ˈfɑːðə/](https://wasscetutor.com/audio/oral/father.mp3?v=6f3f6315b5) [make /meɪk/](https://wasscetutor.com/audio/oral/make.mp3?v=4c4b9660b8)

**Why the other options are wrong**

- c**a**t: The *a* in *cat* is the short vowel /æ/.
- f**a**ther: The *a* in *father* is the long vowel /ɑː/.
- m**a**ke: The *a* in *make* is the diphthong /eɪ/.

questions.stem:
Choose the word that has the same vowel sound as the one represented by the letters in bold.

w**or**d
questions.explanation:
*Word* has the long vowel /ɜː/ of *bird* and *nurse*, the same sound as in *heard*. Many West African speakers say /ɜː/ like /e/ or /a/, so the examination often tests it.

**Listen** (standard British English)

[word /wɜːd/](https://wasscetutor.com/audio/oral/word.mp3?v=f9d785c3cf) [heard /hɜːd/](https://wasscetutor.com/audio/oral/heard.mp3?v=42aa97192e) [ward /wɔːd/](https://wasscetutor.com/audio/oral/ward.mp3?v=3351a8f6a4) [wood /wʊd/](https://wasscetutor.com/audio/oral/wood.mp3?v=2eb25c06e1) [wear /weə/](https://wasscetutor.com/audio/oral/wear.mp3?v=81e608b5c4)

**Why the other options are wrong**

- w**ar**d: *Ward* has /ɔː/, as in *law*, not /ɜː/.
- w**oo**d: *Wood* has /ʊ/, as in *put*.
- w**ear**: *Wear* has the diphthong /eə/, as in *hair*.

questions.stem:
Choose the word that has the same vowel sound as the one represented by the letters in bold.

c**augh**t
questions.explanation:
*Caught* has the long vowel /ɔː/, as in *law*, *port* and *walk*. Telling /ɔː/ from /əʊ/ (*caught / coat*) and from /ɒ/ (*caught / cot*) is a common test.

**Listen** (standard British English)

[caught /kɔːt/](https://wasscetutor.com/audio/oral/caught.mp3?v=4cf92b6eb4) [law /lɔː/](https://wasscetutor.com/audio/oral/law.mp3?v=ab76523aef) [coat /kəʊt/](https://wasscetutor.com/audio/oral/coat.mp3?v=540664177d) [cot /kɒt/](https://wasscetutor.com/audio/oral/cot.mp3?v=7b30587507) [cut /kʌt/](https://wasscetutor.com/audio/oral/cut.mp3?v=36a49b80e1)

**Why the other options are wrong**

- c**oa**t: *Coat* has the diphthong /əʊ/; *caught* has a pure long vowel.
- c**o**t: *Cot* has the short vowel /ɒ/; *caught* has the long /ɔː/.
- c**u**t: *Cut* has /ʌ/.

questions.stem: Which of the following words contains the diphthong /eɪ/?
questions.explanation:
*Great* rhymes with *late* and *weight*: /eɪ/. The letters *ea* spell different sounds in *great*, *bread* and *heart*, and *said* does not rhyme with *paid*.

**Listen** (standard British English)

[great /ɡreɪt/](https://wasscetutor.com/audio/oral/great.mp3?v=80ce7eec8e) [bread /bred/](https://wasscetutor.com/audio/oral/bread.mp3?v=2ad7534c4d) [said /sed/](https://wasscetutor.com/audio/oral/said.mp3?v=cb0195b465) [heart /hɑːt/](https://wasscetutor.com/audio/oral/heart.mp3?v=72d6490041)

**Why the other options are wrong**

- br**ea**d: *Bread* has the pure vowel /e/.
- s**ai**d: *Said* is pronounced /sed/, with the pure vowel /e/, not /eɪ/.
- h**ea**rt: *Heart* has /ɑː/.

papers.title: Consonants and Consonant Clusters: practice set 1
papers.description: 8 original WASSCE-style objective questions on consonants and consonant clusters, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: Which of the following words begins with the sound /θ/?
questions.explanation:
/θ/ is the voiceless *th* of *thin*, *think* and *three*. Its voiced partner /ð/ begins *this*, *these* and *though*. Saying /θ/ as /t/ (*tick* for *thick*) is a common substitution.

**Listen** (standard British English)

[thick /θɪk/](https://wasscetutor.com/audio/oral/thick.mp3?v=84eaed36a1) [these /ðiːz/](https://wasscetutor.com/audio/oral/these.mp3?v=7375766c20) [Thomas /ˈtɒməs/](https://wasscetutor.com/audio/oral/thomas.mp3?v=c13258a6ca) [though /ðəʊ/](https://wasscetutor.com/audio/oral/though.mp3?v=3654f11cf8)

**Why the other options are wrong**

- these: *These* begins with the voiced sound /ð/, as in *this*.
- Thomas: In *Thomas* the *th* is pronounced /t/.
- though: *Though* begins with the voiced sound /ð/.

questions.stem: Which of the following words contains the sound /ʒ/?
questions.explanation:
/ʒ/ is the voiced partner of /ʃ/, heard in *measure*, *pleasure*, *vision* and *television* (/ˈtelɪvɪʒn/). It is rare in English and often replaced by /ʃ/ or /dʒ/.

**Listen** (standard British English)

[television /ˈtelɪvɪʒn/](https://wasscetutor.com/audio/oral/television.mp3?v=fe7a1ea22e) [mission /ˈmɪʃn/](https://wasscetutor.com/audio/oral/mission.mp3?v=93f80730b3) [nation /ˈneɪʃn/](https://wasscetutor.com/audio/oral/nation.mp3?v=2a90f3017b) [pressure /ˈpreʃə/](https://wasscetutor.com/audio/oral/pressure.mp3?v=ff3fcad898)

**Why the other options are wrong**

- mission: *Mission* contains /ʃ/: /ˈmɪʃn/.
- nation: *Nation* contains /ʃ/: /ˈneɪʃn/.
- pressure: *Pressure* contains /ʃ/: /ˈpreʃə/.

questions.stem: In which of the following words is the ending *-ed* pronounced /ɪd/?
questions.explanation:
*-ed* adds a syllable, /ɪd/, only after /t/ or /d/: *land* + *-ed* = /ˈlændɪd/. After other voiceless sounds it is /t/; after voiced sounds it is /d/.

**Listen** (standard British English)

[landed /ˈlændɪd/](https://wasscetutor.com/audio/oral/landed.mp3?v=ccc2d5adf3) [hoped /həʊpt/](https://wasscetutor.com/audio/oral/hoped.mp3?v=0440ad55c6) [begged /beɡd/](https://wasscetutor.com/audio/oral/begged.mp3?v=baab378fc6) [fixed /fɪkst/](https://wasscetutor.com/audio/oral/fixed.mp3?v=8e28f2b33e)

**Why the other options are wrong**

- hoped: *Hope* ends in the voiceless /p/, so *-ed* is /t/: /həʊpt/.
- begged: *Beg* ends in the voiced /g/, so *-ed* is /d/: /beɡd/.
- fixed: *Fix* ends in /s/ (the *x* is /ks/), a voiceless sound, so *-ed* is /t/.

questions.stem: In which of the following words is the final *-s* or *-es* pronounced /ɪz/?
questions.explanation:
The ending adds a syllable, /ɪz/, after the hissing sounds /s/, /z/, /ʃ/, /ʒ/, /tʃ/ and /dʒ/. *Judge* ends in /dʒ/, so *judges* is /ˈdʒʌdʒɪz/.

**Listen** (standard British English)

[judges /ˈdʒʌdʒɪz/](https://wasscetutor.com/audio/oral/judges.mp3?v=d6f584f3dd) [beds /bedz/](https://wasscetutor.com/audio/oral/beds.mp3?v=a2f3625447) [caps /kæps/](https://wasscetutor.com/audio/oral/caps.mp3?v=4366769a33) [rooms /ruːmz/](https://wasscetutor.com/audio/oral/rooms.mp3?v=a750df2eb6)

**Why the other options are wrong**

- beds: *Bed* ends in the voiced /d/, so the ending is /z/.
- caps: *Cap* ends in the voiceless /p/, so the ending is /s/.
- rooms: *Room* ends in the voiced /m/, so the ending is /z/.

questions.stem: Which of the following words contains a silent consonant?
questions.explanation:
In *listen* (/ˈlɪsn/) the *t* is silent, as in *castle* and *whistle*. Other silent consonants: the *k* in *knife*, the *b* in *climb*, the *h* in *hour*.

**Listen** (standard British English)

[listen /ˈlɪsn/](https://wasscetutor.com/audio/oral/listen.mp3?v=38284437a4) [lemon /ˈlemən/](https://wasscetutor.com/audio/oral/lemon.mp3?v=96579ac4d3) [limit /ˈlɪmɪt/](https://wasscetutor.com/audio/oral/limit.mp3?v=3bfa5f9326) [lentil /ˈlentl/](https://wasscetutor.com/audio/oral/lentil.mp3?v=4491558fab)

**Why the other options are wrong**

- lemon: Every consonant in *lemon* is pronounced: /ˈlemən/.
- limit: Every consonant in *limit* is pronounced: /ˈlɪmɪt/.
- lentil: Every consonant in *lentil* is pronounced: /ˈlentl/.

questions.stem: Which of the following words begins with a cluster of three consonant sounds?
questions.explanation:
A cluster is counted in sounds, not letters. *Street* begins with /s/ + /t/ + /r/: three consonant sounds with no vowel between them.

**Listen** (standard British English)

[street /striːt/](https://wasscetutor.com/audio/oral/street.mp3?v=d4569b1177) [sheep /ʃiːp/](https://wasscetutor.com/audio/oral/sheep.mp3?v=6f8eb8e2cb) [photo /ˈfəʊtəʊ/](https://wasscetutor.com/audio/oral/photo.mp3?v=96b1ac88cb) [think /θɪŋk/](https://wasscetutor.com/audio/oral/think.mp3?v=c7c3735bbd)

**Why the other options are wrong**

- sheep: *Sh* is one sound, /ʃ/, so *sheep* begins with a single consonant.
- photo: *Ph* is one sound, /f/.
- think: *Th* is one sound, /θ/.

questions.stem: In which of the following words is *ch* pronounced /k/?
questions.explanation:
*Ch* spells /tʃ/ (*church*), /k/ (*chemistry*, *character*, *school*) or /ʃ/ (*machine*, *chef*).

**Listen** (standard British English)

[chemistry /ˈkemɪstri/](https://wasscetutor.com/audio/oral/chemistry.mp3?v=e85f45cfbe) [church /tʃɜːtʃ/](https://wasscetutor.com/audio/oral/church.mp3?v=d49d23f8e2) [machine /məˈʃiːn/](https://wasscetutor.com/audio/oral/machine.mp3?v=f6fb7f9452) [cheap /tʃiːp/](https://wasscetutor.com/audio/oral/cheap.mp3?v=c11f36bba2)

**Why the other options are wrong**

- church: In *church*, both *ch*s are /tʃ/.
- machine: In *machine*, *ch* is /ʃ/.
- cheap: In *cheap*, *ch* is /tʃ/.

questions.stem:
Choose the word that has the same consonant sound as the one represented by the letters in bold.

na**ti**on
questions.explanation:
The *ti* in *nation* is /ʃ/, the same sound as *sh* in *shop*. Confusing /ʃ/ with /tʃ/ (*shop / chop*, *share / chair*) is a common test.

**Listen** (standard British English)

[nation /ˈneɪʃn/](https://wasscetutor.com/audio/oral/nation.mp3?v=2a90f3017b) [shop /ʃɒp/](https://wasscetutor.com/audio/oral/shop.mp3?v=fe578a17bc) [chop /tʃɒp/](https://wasscetutor.com/audio/oral/chop.mp3?v=625ae3a18c) [measure /ˈmeʒə/](https://wasscetutor.com/audio/oral/measure.mp3?v=d474d766b4) [sun /sʌn/](https://wasscetutor.com/audio/oral/sun.mp3?v=9dd7eb170d)

**Why the other options are wrong**

- **ch**op: *Chop* begins with /tʃ/, not /ʃ/.
- mea**s**ure: The *s* in *measure* is the voiced /ʒ/, not /ʃ/.
- **s**un: *Sun* begins with /s/.

papers.title: Word Stress: practice set 1
papers.description: 8 original WASSCE-style objective questions on word stress, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: Which of the following words is stressed on the first syllable?
questions.explanation:
Two-syllable nouns and adjectives are usually stressed on the first syllable: VILlage, MARket, HAPpy. Many two-syllable verbs stress the second.

**Listen** (standard British English)

[village /ˈvɪlɪdʒ/](https://wasscetutor.com/audio/oral/village.mp3?v=169090293e) [arrive /əˈraɪv/](https://wasscetutor.com/audio/oral/arrive.mp3?v=47233103d9) [complete /kəmˈpliːt/](https://wasscetutor.com/audio/oral/complete.mp3?v=820e4387a3) [believe /bɪˈliːv/](https://wasscetutor.com/audio/oral/believe.mp3?v=51442e67bf)

**Why the other options are wrong**

- arrive: *Arrive* is a verb stressed on the second syllable: arRIVE.
- complete: *Complete* is stressed on the second syllable: comPLETE.
- believe: *Believe* is stressed on the second syllable: beLIEVE.

questions.stem: In which sentence is the word *record* correctly stressed? (The stressed syllable is in capitals.)
questions.explanation:
Many noun–verb pairs are spelt alike but stressed differently: the noun on the first syllable (a REcord, a PREsent), the verb on the second (to reCORD, to preSENT).

**Listen** (standard British English)

[record (verb) /rɪˈkɔːd/](https://wasscetutor.com/audio/oral/record-verb.mp3?v=2245f809e2) [record (noun) /ˈrekɔːd/](https://wasscetutor.com/audio/oral/record-noun.mp3?v=9f1315a701)

**Why the other options are wrong**

- She will REcord the song tomorrow.  
  Here *record* is a verb, so the stress falls on the second syllable.
- He broke the world reCORD.  
  Here *record* is a noun, so the stress falls on the first syllable: REcord.
- The teacher keeps a reCORD of attendance.  
  Here *record* is a noun, so it should be REcord.

options.label: A
options.content: She will REcord the song tomorrow.

options.label: C
options.content: She will reCORD the song tomorrow.

options.label: D
options.content: The teacher keeps a reCORD of attendance.

questions.stem: Which of the following shows the correct stress for *examination*?
questions.explanation:
Words ending in *-tion* and *-sion* are stressed on the syllable just before the ending: examiNAtion, eduCAtion, deCIsion.

**Listen** (standard British English)

[examination /ɪɡˌzæmɪˈneɪʃn/](https://wasscetutor.com/audio/oral/examination.mp3?v=60461f4a35)

**Why the other options are wrong**

- exAMination: The stress is not on the second syllable; *-tion* moves it to the syllable just before.
- EXamination: The first syllable is not stressed.
- examinaTION: The ending *-tion* is never stressed; it is the weak syllable /ʃn/.

questions.stem: Which of the following words is stressed on the second syllable?
questions.explanation:
Words ending in *-ity* are stressed on the syllable just before the ending: aBILity, uniVERsity, elecTRIcity.

**Listen** (standard British English)

[ability /əˈbɪlɪti/](https://wasscetutor.com/audio/oral/ability.mp3?v=da592e74e5) [photograph /ˈfəʊtəɡrɑːf/](https://wasscetutor.com/audio/oral/photograph.mp3?v=02ea741adc) [engineer /ˌendʒɪˈnɪə/](https://wasscetutor.com/audio/oral/engineer.mp3?v=7021464047) [interesting /ˈɪntrɪstɪŋ/](https://wasscetutor.com/audio/oral/interesting.mp3?v=0d9602ae8c)

**Why the other options are wrong**

- photograph: *Photograph* is stressed on the first syllable: PHOtograph.
- engineer: *Engineer* is stressed on the last syllable: engiNEER.
- interesting: *Interesting* is stressed on the first syllable: INteresting.

questions.stem: Which of the following words is stressed on the last syllable?
questions.explanation:
The endings *-eer*, *-ee*, *-ese* and *-ique* take the stress themselves: volunTEER, engiNEER, refuGEE, ChiNESE, uNIQUE.

**Listen** (standard British English)

[volunteer /ˌvɒlənˈtɪə/](https://wasscetutor.com/audio/oral/volunteer.mp3?v=9a92f94cf6) [pencil /ˈpensl/](https://wasscetutor.com/audio/oral/pencil.mp3?v=6935892a34) [calendar /ˈkælɪndə/](https://wasscetutor.com/audio/oral/calendar.mp3?v=fc376f36bd) [family /ˈfæmɪli/](https://wasscetutor.com/audio/oral/family.mp3?v=9665c5949c)

**Why the other options are wrong**

- pencil: *Pencil* is a two-syllable noun stressed on the first syllable: PENcil.
- calendar: *Calendar* is stressed on the first syllable: CALendar.
- family: *Family* is stressed on the first syllable: FAMily.

questions.stem: Which of the following words is correctly stressed? (The stressed syllable is in capitals.)
questions.explanation:
These are words often stressed differently in everyday Sierra Leonean speech. The standard forms are INteresting, FAMily, ADvertise and deVELop.

**Listen** (standard British English)

[interesting /ˈɪntrɪstɪŋ/](https://wasscetutor.com/audio/oral/interesting.mp3?v=0d9602ae8c) [family /ˈfæmɪli/](https://wasscetutor.com/audio/oral/family.mp3?v=9665c5949c) [advertise /ˈædvətaɪz/](https://wasscetutor.com/audio/oral/advertise.mp3?v=b6171f1d42) [develop /dɪˈveləp/](https://wasscetutor.com/audio/oral/develop.mp3?v=f0dd701c42)

**Why the other options are wrong**

- faMIly: The stress in *family* is on the first syllable: FAMily.
- adVERtise: The stress in *advertise* is on the first syllable: ADvertise.
- deveLOP: The stress in *develop* is on the second syllable: deVELop.

questions.stem: Which of the following words is stressed on the third syllable?
questions.explanation:
Words ending in *-ic* are stressed on the syllable just before the ending: e-co-NOM-ic, so the stress falls on the third syllable.

**Listen** (standard British English)

[economic /ˌiːkəˈnɒmɪk/](https://wasscetutor.com/audio/oral/economic.mp3?v=620c93d226) [photography /fəˈtɒɡrəfi/](https://wasscetutor.com/audio/oral/photography.mp3?v=7dafdc2e32) [politics /ˈpɒlɪtɪks/](https://wasscetutor.com/audio/oral/politics.mp3?v=dbea992070) [development /dɪˈveləpmənt/](https://wasscetutor.com/audio/oral/development.mp3?v=2b78def367)

**Why the other options are wrong**

- photography: *Photography* is stressed on the second syllable: phoTOgraphy.
- politics: *Politics* is stressed on the first syllable: POlitics.
- development: *Development* is stressed on the second syllable: deVELopment.

questions.stem: Which of the following words has the same stress pattern as *beGIN*?
questions.explanation:
*Begin* has two syllables with the stress on the second. *Decide* (deCIDE) has the same pattern.

**Listen** (standard British English)

[begin /bɪˈɡɪn/](https://wasscetutor.com/audio/oral/begin.mp3?v=3e92f9f112) [decide /dɪˈsaɪd/](https://wasscetutor.com/audio/oral/decide.mp3?v=367b6134f2) [table /ˈteɪbl/](https://wasscetutor.com/audio/oral/table.mp3?v=37d79fe7ea) [open /ˈəʊpən/](https://wasscetutor.com/audio/oral/open.mp3?v=e78ab020d8) [market /ˈmɑːkɪt/](https://wasscetutor.com/audio/oral/market.mp3?v=ead05dd275)

**Why the other options are wrong**

- table: *Table* is stressed on the first syllable: TAble.
- open: *Open* is a verb, but it is one of the exceptions stressed on the first syllable: OPen.
- market: *Market* is a noun stressed on the first syllable: MARket.

papers.title: Sentence Stress and Intonation: practice set 1
papers.description: 8 original WASSCE-style objective questions on sentence stress and intonation, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem:
In the sentence below, the word in capitals carries the emphatic stress.

*My brother SOLD the car.*

Which question does the sentence answer?
questions.explanation:
Emphatic stress falls on the word that corrects the question. SOLD corrects the action: not *buy*, but *sold*.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Did your sister sell the car?  
  This question would be answered by stressing BROTHER, to correct *sister*.
- Did your brother sell the bicycle?  
  This question would be answered by stressing CAR, to correct *bicycle*.
- Did your brother sell the car yesterday?  
  Nothing in this question is corrected by the stress on SOLD.

options.label: A
options.content: Did your sister sell the car?

options.label: B
options.content: Did your brother buy the car?

options.label: C
options.content: Did your brother sell the bicycle?

options.label: D
options.content: Did your brother sell the car yesterday?

questions.stem: A pupil is asked: *Did Musa travel to Bo on Monday?* The pupil answers: *No, Musa travelled to Bo on Tuesday.* Which word in the answer should carry the emphatic stress?
questions.explanation:
Find the detail that changes between question and answer: *Monday* becomes *Tuesday*, so TUESDAY is stressed.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Musa: Musa is not being corrected: the question already names him.
- travelled: The action is not being corrected: he did travel.
- Bo: The place is not being corrected: he did go to Bo.

questions.stem: Which of the following would normally be spoken with a rising tune at the end?
questions.explanation:
Yes/no questions rise at the end. Statements, commands, wh- questions and exclamations fall.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Where are you going?  
  Wh- questions normally have a falling tune: the question word already shows it is a question.
- Close the door.  
  Commands have a falling tune.
- What a lovely dress!  
  Exclamations have a falling tune.

options.label: D
options.content: Are you coming to the match?

questions.stem: A speaker says: *It's very hot today, isn't it?* with a falling tune on the tag. The speaker
questions.explanation:
Falling tag: the speaker is sure and invites agreement. Rising tag: the speaker is unsure and is asking.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- is not sure and is really asking for information: A real question is shown by a rising tune on the tag.
- is angry with the listener: The tune of the tag shows certainty, not anger.
- has not finished the sentence: A falling tune sounds complete; an unfinished statement rises.

options.label: A
options.content: is sure and expects the listener to agree

options.label: B
options.content: is not sure and is really asking for information

questions.stem:
In normal speech, which words carry the stress in this sentence?

*The boys are playing football in the field.*
questions.explanation:
Content words (nouns, main verbs, adjectives, adverbs) carry the stress; function words (articles, auxiliaries, prepositions, pronouns) are weak. This gives English its rhythm.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- The, are, in, the: These are function words, which are normally weak and unstressed.
- boys, are, in, field: *Are* and *in* are function words, normally unstressed.
- Every word is stressed equally: Giving every word equal weight is not the rhythm of standard English.

questions.stem:
How is the list in this sentence normally spoken?

*I bought rice, oil, onions and pepper.*
questions.explanation:
Each item but the last rises, showing more is coming; the last falls, showing the list is complete.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Falling on every item: Falling on each item would make each one sound like the end of the sentence.
- Rising on every item, including *pepper*: A rise on the last item would make the list sound unfinished.
- Rising only on *pepper*: The last item falls, to show the list is complete.

options.label: C
options.content: Rising on *rice*, *oil* and *onions*, and falling on *pepper*

questions.stem:
The word in capitals carries the emphatic stress.

*I didn't say SHE took the money.*

What does the speaker mean?
questions.explanation:
Moving the stress changes the meaning, because the stressed word is the one being contrasted. Stress on SHE contrasts her with another person.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Someone else, not the speaker, said it: That meaning needs the stress on I: *I didn't say she took the money.*
- The speaker suggested it but did not actually say it: That meaning needs the stress on SAY.
- She borrowed the money; she did not take it: That meaning needs the stress on TOOK.

options.label: A
options.content: Someone else, not the speaker, said it

options.label: B
options.content: The speaker suggested it but did not actually say it

options.label: C
options.content: She borrowed the money; she did not take it

options.label: D
options.content: Someone else, not she, took the money

questions.stem: *You failed the test?* spoken with a sharp rising tune expresses
questions.explanation:
This is an echo question: a statement repeated with a rising tune to show surprise or to check what was heard.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- complete certainty: Certainty is shown by a falling tune.
- a command: Commands have a falling tune.
- the end of a list: The end of a list has a falling tune.

papers.title: Listening Comprehension Skills: practice set 1
papers.description: 8 original WASSCE-style objective questions on listening comprehension skills, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: In the few seconds before a listening passage is read, the most useful thing a candidate can do is to
questions.explanation:
Knowing the questions tells you what to listen for: a time, a name, a reason. Then you can predict and note details briefly.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- try to write down every word that will be read: No one can write down every word; it means missing the meaning.
- close the eyes and wait for the passage to begin: This wastes the only chance to prepare.
- start answering the questions by guessing: Answers should come from the passage, not from guessing in advance.

options.label: A
options.content: try to write down every word that will be read

options.label: B
options.content: read the questions and mark the key words to listen for

options.label: C
options.content: close the eyes and wait for the passage to begin

options.label: D
options.content: start answering the questions by guessing

questions.stem:
A speaker says:

[Play the passage](https://wasscetutor.com/audio/oral/eng-lis-02.mp3?v=86adbea5a5)

> Many people think the market opens at eight o'clock. However, it actually opens at nine.

At what time does the market open?
questions.explanation:
Signal words such as *however*, *actually* and *in fact* warn that a correction is coming, and the correction is usually the answer. Test-setters often put the first-mentioned detail in a wrong option.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Eight o'clock: Eight is what people *think*; *however* signals the correction.
- Half past eight: No such time is mentioned.
- The speaker does not say: The speaker clearly says the market opens at nine.

questions.stem:
The following conversation is read aloud.

[Play the conversation](https://wasscetutor.com/audio/oral/eng-lis-03.mp3?v=629825f98a)

> **Man:** Take two tablets three times a day, after meals, and finish the whole course.
>
> **Woman:** Even if I feel better after two days?
>
> **Man:** Yes, even then. And come back if the fever returns.

What is the most likely relationship between the speakers?
questions.explanation:
Inference comes from clues: *tablets*, *three times a day*, *finish the whole course* and *the fever* all point to medicine being given out.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- A teacher and a pupil: Nothing about lessons or school is mentioned.
- A trader and a buyer of rice: They are talking about tablets and a fever, not rice.
- A driver and a passenger: Nothing about a journey or a vehicle is mentioned.

options.label: B
options.content: A trader and a buyer of rice

questions.stem:
The following conversation is read aloud.

[Play the conversation](https://wasscetutor.com/audio/oral/eng-lis-04.mp3?v=80e721b0bb)

> **Man:** How much are the oranges?
>
> **Woman:** NLe 20 for ten.
>
> **Man:** I'll take twenty, and that pineapple.
>
> **Woman:** The pineapple is NLe 15.

How much does the man pay altogether?
questions.explanation:
Twenty oranges at NLe 20 for ten cost NLe 40; with the pineapple, 40 + 15 = NLe 55. The total is never spoken: you must combine two details.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- NLe 15: NLe 15 is the price of the pineapple alone.
- NLe 35: This counts ten oranges instead of twenty: 20 + 15.
- NLe 40: NLe 40 is the price of the twenty oranges alone, without the pineapple.

questions.stem:
A speaker says, slowly:

[Play the passage](https://wasscetutor.com/audio/oral/eng-lis-05.mp3?v=b2ac2be9ca)

> Well... I suppose I could help you move on Saturday, if there's really nobody else.

How does the speaker feel about helping?
questions.explanation:
*Well...*, *I suppose* and the condition *if there's really nobody else*, said slowly, all show reluctance. Attitude comes from the words and the voice.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Enthusiastic: An eager helper would agree at once, not say *I suppose* and *if there's really nobody else*.
- Angry: Nothing the speaker says shows anger.
- Relieved: Being relieved does not fit offering help unwillingly.

questions.stem:
A speaker at a school meeting says:

[Play the passage](https://wasscetutor.com/audio/oral/eng-lis-06.mp3?v=a7ce6ec15f)

> Last year, three pupils from this very school were injured crossing the highway. That is why we are asking the council to build a footbridge.

Why does the speaker mention the three injured pupils?
questions.explanation:
*That is why* links the accident to the request: the injuries are evidence for the footbridge. Purpose questions ask why a detail is included.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- To praise the three pupils: Nothing in the talk praises them.
- To announce the pupils' names: No names are given.
- To ask pupils to stop using the highway: The speaker asks the council for a footbridge, not pupils to avoid the road.

options.label: B
options.content: To show why a footbridge is needed

options.label: D
options.content: To ask pupils to stop using the highway

questions.stem:
The following announcement is read aloud.

[Play the announcement](https://wasscetutor.com/audio/oral/eng-lis-07.mp3?v=e8d9bbad3b)

> Good morning. From Monday, the library will open at eight o'clock instead of nine, and close at six. Pupils may now borrow three books at a time instead of two, and books may be kept for two weeks.

What is the announcement mainly about?
questions.explanation:
The main idea covers all the details: new times, more books, a longer loan. Each wrong option fits only part of the passage or none of it.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- The opening of a new library: The library already exists; only its rules are changing.
- How to find a book in the library: Finding books is not mentioned.
- The closing of the library: The library is not closing; it is opening earlier.

options.label: A
options.content: The opening of a new library

options.label: B
options.content: How to find a book in the library

options.label: C
options.content: Changes to the library's opening times and borrowing rules

questions.stem: In a listening test, one option repeats several words exactly as the speaker said them. What should the candidate do?
questions.explanation:
Judge every option by the meaning of what was said, not by matching words. Eliminate what you know is wrong, then choose.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Choose it at once, because it uses the speaker's words: Wrong options often reuse the speaker's words in a way that changes the meaning.
- Reject it at once, because the right answer never repeats the speaker's words: The right answer may repeat the speaker's words; the point is to check the meaning.
- Leave the question blank: A blank earns nothing; eliminate options and choose the best one.

options.label: A
options.content: Choose it at once, because it uses the speaker's words

options.label: B
options.content: Reject it at once, because the right answer never repeats the speaker's words

options.label: D
options.content: Check that the option matches the meaning, because repeated words are often a trap
